items.prompt: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list.
items.why: k sorted lists merged in order → a min-heap of the k heads, refilled from the list you just popped.

items.prompt: Merge two sorted arrays into one sorted array.
items.why: Only two lists → compare the two heads with two pointers. A heap of 2 adds a log factor for nothing.

items.prompt: Given m sorted arrays and k, return the k-th smallest number among all of them.
items.why: The arrays are already sorted, so pop the smallest head k times. A size-k heap over every element (Top K) ignores that order and reads all N.

items.prompt: Return the k-th largest element of an unsorted array.
items.why: One unsorted collection, nothing pre-sorted to merge → a size-k min-heap (Top 'K' Elements).

items.prompt: Given k sorted lists, find the smallest range [a, b] that includes at least one number from each list.
items.why: One element per list in a min-heap plus the running max: the range is [top, max], and you advance the list that holds the min. 'From each of k sorted lists' decides it.

items.prompt: Given the work schedules of several employees (each a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals), return the intervals when everyone is free.
items.why: The question is about overlaps and gaps between intervals → Merge Intervals. You may merge the schedules by start time first, but the overlap sweep is the core.

items.prompt: Given two sorted arrays and k, return the k pairs (one element from each array) with the smallest sums.
items.why: Each a[i] defines a sorted list a[i] + b[0], a[i] + b[1], … → k-way merge over those implicit lists, stopping after k pops.

items.prompt: Given two sorted arrays of sizes m and n, return the median of their union in O(log(m + n)) time.
items.why: The logarithmic bound rules out walking the merged order (that's O(m + n)). Binary search on the partition point instead.
